Avalanche construction has researcher degrees of freedom. Freeze graph sampling, thresholds, regression support, and synthetic Gaussian controls.
Finite attention experiments may be too small to determine transition order. Treat absence of registered size scaling as a failed phase claim, not weak positive evidence.
A heterogeneous tournament can encourage vague synthesis. Preserve paper-specific estimands and allow different mechanisms to win in different regimes.
first_week: Reproduce one modular-addition grokking run and implement a strictly causal feature logger with no future-alignment API.
Clone 12 checkpoints into true, fixed-dose, replayed, randomized, and covariance-matched trigger arms and verify dose balance.
Implement censored transition labels, horizon AUPRC, survival calibration, and cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals.
Run synchronized four-width avalanche probes plus Gaussian and width-support controls to estimate measurement variance.
Preregister feature definitions, hazard model size, held-out moduli and attention variants, escape-law comparison, and decisive claim blockers.

competitive_landscape.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
competitive_landscape.difference: The original work establishes delayed generalization and regularization sensitivity; this proposal tests whether later criticality signals add prospective and causal information.

competitive_landscape.title: Omnigrok: Grokking Beyond Algorithmic Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Omnigrok links grokking across tasks to weight norm and fixed regularization. Weight and norm baselines therefore must lose before a criticality certificate can claim value.

competitive_landscape.title: Progress Measures for Grokking via Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: Mechanistic circuit measures precede behavioral generalization. The tournament compares their held-out forecast and intervention value directly with scalar criticality signals.

competitive_landscape.title: Information-Theoretic Progress Measures reveal Grokking is an Emergent Phase Transition
competitive_landscape.difference: The information measure targets structured compression before generalization. It becomes a preregistered single-observable baseline rather than an omitted alternative.

competitive_landscape.title: From Density Matrices to Phase Transitions in Deep Learning: Spectral Early Warnings and Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: This work proposes 2RDM spectral warnings across induction and grokking. The tournament asks whether they forecast untouched transitions and add to simpler state variables.

competitive_landscape.title: Thermodynamic Isomorphism of Transformers: A Lagrangian Approach to Attention Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper supplies the attention-temperature and specific-heat framing but reports finite-size crossover qualifications. The proposal makes those finite-size gates mandatory.

competitive_landscape.title: Toward a Physics of Deep Learning and Brains
competitive_landscape.difference: This work already applies avalanche distributions, susceptibility, and finite-size scaling. The proposed synchronized, past-only test asks whether a fitted dimension carries incremental transition information.

competitive_landscape.title: Power-law escape rate of SGD
competitive_landscape.difference: Multiplicative MSE SGD noise predicts power-law escape governed by a log-loss barrier. The factorial noise experiment directly compares this account with a simple Arrhenius fit.

competitive_landscape.title: Phase Transitions between Accuracy Regimes in L2 regularized Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This earlier work studies L2-induced phases, local minima, hysteresis, and grokking-like jumps. The tournament isolates whether prepared deep-linear escape generalizes beyond that narrow landscape.

competitive_landscape.title: Grokking as a First Order Phase Transition in Two Layer Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This theory derives competition between memorizing and generalizing solutions. It sets a higher bar for phase language than temporal coincidence with an observable peak.

competitive_landscape.title: Is Grokking a Computational Glass Relaxation?
competitive_landscape.difference: The computational-glass account emphasizes rugged high-norm solutions and cases without a simple entropy barrier. Held-out escape-law tests distinguish it from a universal barrier narrative.

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
competitive_landscape.difference: Induction heads and their abrupt formation were established in causal multi-layer models. The proposed attention arm tests whether a fused one-layer copy transition survives realistic factorization and causality.

competitive_landscape.title: Predicting the Emergence of Induction Heads in Language Model Pretraining
competitive_landscape.difference: This work explicitly predicts induction-head emergence in pretraining, so claims that softmax copy transitions are intrinsically unpredictable require a direct held-out comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Regularization of Gradient Flow on One-Layer Softmax Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: Separately trained key and query matrices have nuclear-norm implicit regularization unlike the fused Gaussian matrix. The held-out factorized arm tests whether the predicted transition order is structural or prior-specific.

brief.novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after four hash-pinned, page-anchored readings and an 18-paper focused panel: grokking, norm and regularization accounts, mechanistic and information progress measures, spectral warnings, thermodynamic observables, neural avalanches, stochastic escape laws, landscape phases, induction-head transitions, and factorized-attention regularization are established. The narrow contribution is not a new criticality statistic; it is a preregistered past-only forecast tournament coupled to identical-checkpoint causal interventions and explicit finite-size claim gates.
brief.evidence_note: Supported by four current full-text readings totaling 85 pages, with 66 page-anchored findings, 130 anchors, and 45 checked competitor entries spanning 33 unique primary papers.

factors.rationale: Requires a fresh experimental scaffold derived from public paper specifications.

The decisive full-batch and small-network experiments are tractable, but repeated eigensolves, exact selector estimates, checkpoint-by-group branches, seed replication, and held-out optimizer and architecture arms create a meaningful compute budget.

Identical-checkpoint branches, a fixed-eta sharp-subspace intervention, random- and stable-subspace controls, matched first-order progress, preregistered groups, and signed allocation outcomes provide unusually direct pass/fail criteria.

EoS, sharp-mode dynamics, outlier effects, stochastic and non-Euclidean boundaries, and same-checkpoint interventions are established. The defensible novelty is isolating post-entry subgroup allocation with a curvature-specific clamp, not proposing another transition signal or stability law.

A smooth positive control and binary-CIFAR falsification can resolve the central confound quickly; stable multi-mode, momentum, Adam-metric, held-out architecture, and scale conclusions require longer instrumentation and replication.

assumptions: A leading unstable Hessian subspace with a registered eigengap can be estimated accurately enough to intervene on small full-batch models.
Constrained compensation in the stable subspace can match total update norm and first-order aggregate descent closely enough that residual imbalance is measured rather than hidden.
Data groups can be fixed without using branch outcomes, future losses, or the selector being evaluated.
Exact sharpness-gradient selectors are computationally feasible on the smooth development models, while nonsmooth and stochastic extensions are treated as separate estimands.
Optimizer-generic language is blocked unless the intervention is rebuilt in the relevant momentum, adaptive, or zeroth-order stability geometry.

brief.title: Curvature-clamped allocation at the edge of stability
brief.thesis: After edge-of-stability entry has already occurred, branch from identical checkpoints while holding the nominal learning rate, future data stream, and orthogonal update fixed; selectively damp only the empirically unstable Hessian subspace and compare with equal-rank random-subspace, stable-subspace, update-norm-matched, first-order-progress-matched, and eta/2 exit controls. EoS counts as a subgroup-allocation mechanism only if the true sharp-subspace clamp changes the registered vector of group progress in the direction predicted by the exact sharpness selector and the effect survives held-out groups, widths, and a separately derived optimizer geometry.
brief.motivation: The closest paper reports that continuing at EoS favors some constructed data groups while halving eta favors others, but that fork changes ordinary learning speed, truncation error, path, and the exit branch's stability threshold. Its empirical squared top-eigenvector alignment is also only a proxy for the theoretical third-derivative selector. The other three full readings sharpen the caution: current-state norm criticality can collapse algebraically to the usual sharpness boundary and is gauge-dependent; exact finite-step curvature identities force a threshold average only under persistent step energy and locate curvature at unobserved interior points; and conservation-law drift does not establish a valid universal spectral mechanism. A fixed-eta, mode-specific causal intervention can test the narrow distributional claim without becoming another retrospective criticality statistic or learning-rate comparison.
brief.research_question: Once a run is already at EoS, does suppressing only its unstable curvature subspace at fixed nominal eta causally redistribute learning progress across preregistered data groups beyond ordinary step-size, update-dose, random-direction, subgroup-difficulty, and optimizer-geometry explanations?
non_claims: The project does not propose a new early-warning signal, forecast transition time, trigger grokking, or search for a universal criticality order parameter.
It does not claim that EoS is universally beneficial; extra progress on deliberately corrupted labels can be harmful.
It does not treat squared alignment C_k=(grad l_k dot v_1)^2 as identical to the theoretical selector Q_k=<grad l_k,grad S>.
It does not assume the Euclidean full-batch threshold 2/eta applies unchanged to momentum, SGD, Adam, weight decay, normalization, or zeroth-order optimization.
It does not infer a causal mechanism from a current-state algebraic boundary, a step-energy-weighted asymptote, eigendirection localization, or conservation-law drift alone.
It does not claim that a one-mode intervention is meaningful when the leading subspace reorganizes, localizes, lacks an eigengap, or contains several unstable modes.
A small-model mechanism result is not a large-model or universal scaling result.
subquestions: Does a fixed-eta sharp-subspace clamp change group loss and margin progress more than an equal-rank random- or stable-subspace clamp with matched removed energy?
After aggregate linear descent, total update norm, orthogonal update, future minibatches, and branch length are matched, does a residual group-allocation effect remain?
Does exact Q_k prospectively predict the signed clamp effect and rank groups better than C_k, gradient norm, margin, centroid distance, loss, and label-noise indicators?
Do results require a simple stable v_1, or do they transfer when a registered rank-r spectral projector is used under eigenvalue crossings and near-degeneracy?
Do natural clean-hard and tail groups behave like constructed input or output outliers, and is any gain accompanied by improved clean, balanced, robust, or tail generalization?
How do the estimand and intervention change for minibatch SGD with momentum, Adam-like preconditioning, and zeroth-order methods whose boundary depends on the full spectrum and trace?
method: Begin with a C3 smooth full-batch regression or classification positive control where the full Hessian, leading eigenspace, sharpness gradient grad S, Q_k, and every finite-step remainder can be computed exactly or to tight numerical tolerance.

Reproduce the binary CIFAR-10 width-512 MLP setup with MSE and the same-checkpoint eta versus eta/2 fork, but fix groups before branching: clean inliers, kNN-ambiguous boundary points, randomized output labels, bounded valid-range coherent input shifts, equal-distance random shifts, rare classes or subpopulations, and natural margin or centroid-distance deciles.

Declare post-entry checkpoints from current and past aggregate states only, using a registered run of leading curvature at or above the full-batch threshold; do not fit a transition forecast, align runs on future spikes, or use later subgroup outcomes to choose checkpoints.

Estimate the smallest leading projector P_t whose registered eigenvalues are unstable and require an eigengap plus projector-overlap stability. If the subspace is not stable, abstain from a one-mode claim and analyze a wider projector or reject the intervention for that checkpoint.

Construct a clamped candidate update by replacing the baseline coefficient of P_t g with a registered stable coefficient while leaving (I-P_t)g unchanged. Add a constrained stable-subspace compensation arm that matches baseline total update norm and aggregate g-transpose-delta within tolerance, and record any infeasible residual imbalance.

From each checkpoint run the same future examples through baseline EoS, eta/2 exit, true sharp-subspace clamp, equal-rank random-subspace clamp, stable-eigenvector clamp, removed-energy replay, and norm-plus-linear-progress-matched compensation branches. Recompute or freeze P_t on a registered schedule and treat these as distinct estimands.

Measure groupwise cumulative loss and margin change, the whole-training loss, clean and balanced accuracy, corrupted-label fit, and exact Q_k versus proxy C_k before opening branch outcomes. Fit a sparse signed allocation model on development seeds and freeze group definitions, rank r, doses, matching tolerances, horizons, and exclusions.

Open log-spaced held-out widths and a BatchNorm-free ResNet-14 or small synthetic Transformer only after the full-batch protocol is frozen. For SGD with momentum, use the registered stochastic or state-augmented stability operator rather than raw full-Hessian v_1; treat Adam as a separate preconditioned-metric experiment because its leading eigenvectors can reorganize and localize.

Do not transfer the top-mode intervention to zeroth-order optimization. A ZO diagnostic, if run on the smallest models, must use its full-spectrum or lambda-max-plus-trace mean-square stability condition and is a negative transfer test, not confirmation of the first-order mechanism.

validation_funnel.stage: Numerical identity and smooth positive control
validation_funnel.gate: Lanczos and autodiff recover the full-Hessian subspace and exact Q_k within tolerance; the clamp changes only the registered subspace; norm, linear-descent, and data-stream matching residuals are published.

At identical post-entry checkpoints, true sharp-subspace damping changes the signed group-allocation vector beyond eta/2, random-subspace, stable-subspace, removed-energy, and matched-progress controls.

The frozen selector and intervention transfer from constructed groups to preregistered natural difficulty or tail strata, with clean, balanced, robustness, and corrupted-label outcomes reported separately.

The effect survives an untouched width and architecture only where leading-projector stability passes; any momentum or Adam claim uses a separately derived operator, and no first-order result is asserted for ZO.

scaling_claim_protocol.answer: Small full-batch models can identify or falsify a post-entry allocation mechanism, but they cannot establish optimizer-generic or large-scale EoS behavior. Freeze the group taxonomy, intervention construction, subspace-stability test, Q and C estimators, matching tolerances, horizons, and statistical model before opening the largest width, second architecture, and optimizer-specific arm.
supporting_evidence: Across untouched widths and the second architecture, the true sharp-subspace clamp retains the registered signed allocation effect beyond every random-, stable-, energy-, norm-, and linear-progress-matched control.
Exact Q_k predicts held-out clamp-effect sign and rank beyond C_k, margin, loss, group gradient norm, centroid distance, and checkpoint age without threshold refitting.
Projector overlap, eigengap, and localization remain within preregistered validity bounds; abstentions predict where the one-mode account fails rather than being dropped.

The group effect is not merely extra fitting of corrupted labels: clean, balanced, tail, and robustness endpoints move in the registered direction or the claim is explicitly limited to allocation of training loss.
Momentum or Adam results reproduce only after the stability operator and clamp are defined in the appropriate stochastic, state-space, or preconditioned metric.
claim_blockers: The true clamp does not beat equal-rank random- or stable-subspace clamps after update norm, aggregate linear descent, future data, and branch horizon are matched.
Exact Q_k fails to predict signed held-out effects or adds no value beyond C_k and simple difficulty, gradient, or loss baselines.
The leading projector has no reproducible eigengap, its overlap falls below the registered stability tolerance, or results reverse when rank r is widened.
Adam-like training exhibits persistent leading-eigenvector reorganization or localization and a Euclidean clamp is nevertheless required to recover the result.
An SGD or momentum result disappears when the batch-distribution or momentum-state stability operator replaces raw full-Hessian v_1.
A zeroth-order result requires only lambda_max damping even though the registered mean-square boundary depends materially on the full spectrum or Hessian trace.
Effects are confined to intentionally wrong labels, invalid off-manifold inputs, one seed, one hand-selected checkpoint, or one width.
Held-out width or architecture reverses the signed allocation vector or requires group-, optimizer-, or scale-specific retuning.
Residual mismatch in g-transpose-delta, total norm, data exposure, or whole-loss progress explains the apparent group effect.
prospective_design: Develop exact-Q estimation, projector tracking, and constrained compensation on smooth models and two smaller MLP widths.
Freeze all groups, thresholds, subspace ranks, matching tolerances, branch horizons, seed rules, exclusions, and effect-size tests before the main width is evaluated.
Keep the largest width, a BatchNorm-free ResNet or small Transformer, natural group definitions, and optimizer-specific operator unopened until the fixed-eta causal gate passes.
Publish every checkpoint including eigenspace-abstention cases, optimizer failures, negative generalization effects, and mismatched-control diagnostics.
why_small_models_fail: The leading Hessian direction can rotate, become localized, or split into a cluster as architecture, optimizer, normalization, width, and training time change.
Full-batch group gradients and exact third derivatives are observable on small models but prohibitively expensive and noisier under minibatch training.
Constructed binary-CIFAR outliers can be off-manifold and need not represent long-tail, ambiguous, corrupted, or rare examples in natural data.
Momentum and Adam introduce optimizer state and a different metric; ZO mean-square stability depends on the full spectrum and trace rather than only lambda_max.
Small-model EoS may be a single-mode oscillation, whereas wider or deeper models can have several unstable modes and residual or normalization-induced gauge effects.
scaling_claim_protocol.claim_language: If only the smooth and binary-CIFAR gates pass, claim a fixed-eta causal subgroup-allocation effect for full-batch GD in those models. Claim architecture transfer only if the frozen projector and group gates pass untouched. Claim optimizer transfer separately and only with the registered optimizer-specific stability operator. Never describe the result as a transition forecast, universal benefit of EoS, universal lambda-max law, or evidence for ZO from a first-order clamp.

experiment.primary_hypothesis: At identical post-entry full-batch-GD checkpoints, damping the registered unstable Hessian projector at fixed nominal eta will change the vector of groupwise cumulative loss progress more than equal-rank random- and stable-subspace damping after total update norm, aggregate first-order descent, future data, and branch horizon are matched; exact Q_k will predict the signed difference out of sample better than C_k and simple group-difficulty baselines.
experiment.secondary_hypothesis: The frozen signed allocation model will transfer to an untouched width and architecture only when leading-projector stability passes, while momentum, Adam, and zeroth-order arms will require their own stability geometry and will falsify any optimizer-generic Euclidean-v_1 claim.
domains: C3 smooth synthetic regression or classification with an exactly computable Hessian and sharpness gradient
Binary CIFAR-10 width-swept two-hidden-layer MLP with MSE and full-batch GD
Preregistered natural clean-hard, boundary, rare, randomized-label, bounded coherent-shift, and matched random-shift groups
An untouched BatchNorm-free ResNet-14 or four-layer synthetic Transformer architecture
A separately analyzed minibatch-SGD-with-momentum arm; exploratory Adam-metric and smallest-model ZO negative-transfer diagnostics
baselines: Continued EoS at eta and the original eta/2 exit fork
No intervention and an equal-horizon ordinary full-batch-GD branch
Equal-rank random-subspace, stable-eigenvector, and bottom-spectrum clamps
Removed sharp-component energy replayed in a random stable direction
Total-update-norm-only matching and joint norm-plus-g-transpose-delta constrained matching
Frozen versus periodically recomputed leading projector
Exact Q_k, empirical C_k, group gradient norm, current group loss, margin, centroid distance, kNN ambiguity, label status, and elapsed-step predictors
Raw full-Hessian, batch-distribution, momentum-state, preconditioned-metric, and full-spectrum-or-trace stability definitions where applicable
ablations: Rank-one v_1 versus the full registered unstable rank-r projector
Remove eigengap and projector-overlap abstention to quantify selection bias from unstable modes
Remove norm matching, linear-descent matching, data-stream matching, or whole-loss adjustment one at a time
Constructed prototype groups versus natural fixed strata and valid-range versus off-range input shifts
Exact third-derivative Q_k versus C_k alone and versus a sparse combined predictor
GELU or other smooth activation versus ReLU and full-batch GD versus minibatch SGD with momentum
Euclidean top mode versus optimizer-specific generalized mode in Adam-like training
Top-eigenvalue clamp versus the full-spectrum or lambda-max-plus-trace condition in the ZO diagnostic
experiment.primary_outcome: The checkpoint-blocked difference-in-differences allocation vector: each group's cumulative loss and margin change under the true sharp-subspace clamp minus baseline EoS, relative to the same contrast for matched random- and stable-subspace controls, with whole-training progress and matching residuals reported jointly.
experiment.analysis: Use checkpoint, seed, and group as crossed effects; estimate paired allocation contrasts with seed-clustered or hierarchical-bootstrap intervals; evaluate Q and C prospectively with sign accuracy, rank correlation, calibration slope, and incremental held-out log score; correct the fixed group-outcome family for multiplicity; model eigenspace abstentions and optimizer failures rather than dropping them. Predeclare a minimum meaningful standardized allocation contrast and matching tolerance from the smooth pilot, then freeze them before held-out runs.
experiment.decision_rule: Pass the narrow mechanism only if the true sharp-subspace clamp beats every matched random- and stable-subspace control on the preregistered allocation vector with a positive paired interval, exact Q_k improves held-out signed prediction beyond C_k and simple baselines, matching residuals cannot explain the result, and the effect repeats on natural groups at an untouched width. Extend the claim to a second architecture or optimizer only if its separate frozen gate passes. Otherwise report a learning-rate effect, a correlational alignment, an optimizer-specific boundary, or a null result and reject EoS-specific subgroup allocation.

evaluation: Groupwise cumulative loss, margin, accuracy, and gradient-magnitude change over equal data and branch horizons
Checkpoint-blocked allocation difference-in-differences against random-, stable-, energy-, norm-, and linear-progress-matched controls
Q_k and C_k sign accuracy, rank correlation, calibration, incremental log score, and coefficient stability
Whole-training loss, g-transpose-delta, update norm, removed sharp-component energy, Taylor residual, and function-space output change
Leading eigenvalues, eigengap, rank-r projector overlap, eigenvector displacement, inverse-participation localization, and unstable-mode count
Clean, balanced, tail, corrupted-label, bounded-shift, and robustness outcomes reported separately
Cross-width and cross-architecture effect-sign stability, abstention rate, and optimizer-specific replication
Hessian-vector, third-derivative, per-group-gradient, wall-time, memory, and branch-compute costs
falsifiers: Equal-rank random- or stable-subspace damping reproduces the group allocation effect.
The eta/2 branch changes allocation but the fixed-eta sharp-subspace clamp does not.
Norm, aggregate linear-descent, data-stream, or whole-loss mismatches explain the effect.
Exact Q_k has the wrong sign, fails held-out calibration, or adds nothing beyond C_k, current loss, gradient norm, or margin.
The effect vanishes under a rank-r projector, projector-overlap gate, or a second eigensolver tolerance.
Only intentionally wrong labels or invalid input shifts benefit, with no registered natural-group analogue.
Clean, balanced, tail, or robustness outcomes worsen enough to refute any beneficial-allocation language.
The signed allocation vector reverses at the untouched width or architecture without a preregistered abstention condition.
Adam's reorganizing or localized leading subspace, or the correct stochastic/momentum operator, eliminates the Euclidean-v_1 effect.
ZO behavior follows a full-spectrum or trace boundary and is not changed by the first-order top-mode clamp.

human_in_the_loop.answer: Humans are unnecessary for branch assignment, curvature estimation, update matching, executable labels, or quantitative outcomes. They are useful only for a blinded construct-validity audit of natural ambiguity, semantic rarity, and whether bounded input transformations remain recognizable and label preserving.
humans_not_needed_for: EoS checkpoint detection, Hessian and selector computation, randomization, branch execution, matching diagnostics, and statistical analysis
Randomized-label groups, exact synthetic groups, deterministic data provenance, and clean or balanced accuracy
Choosing favorable checkpoints, eigenspace ranks, intervention doses, thresholds, exclusions, or claim language after outcomes are visible
humans_needed_for: Blindly audit a fixed random sample of natural boundary, rare, and coherent-shift examples for semantic validity and label preservation
Adjudicate preregistered automatic-audit disagreements without seeing intervention arm or group-effect estimates
Flag group definitions whose apparent rarity or ambiguity is a dataset artifact rather than a meaningful data-distribution property
human_in_the_loop.measurement: Report audit minutes, sample rate, inter-rater agreement, label-preservation rate, disagreement strata, and results with all mechanically defined groups versus the subset passing blinded semantic audit. Human judgments validate group construction only and never enter the optimizer or selector objective.

risks: A clamp necessarily changes the candidate update. Use random-, stable-, energy-, norm-, and linear-progress-matched arms and publish residual imbalance instead of asserting perfect isolation.

Exact Q_k requires third derivatives and a simple differentiable leading eigenvalue. Use smooth positive controls, rank-r projectors, finite-difference checks, and treat ReLU estimates as separate empirical proxies.
Leading modes may rotate or localize, especially under Adam. Register projector displacement and localization abstention gates and do not hide rejected checkpoints.
Repeated eigensolves can use substantial compute and introduce numerical researcher degrees of freedom. Freeze Lanczos tolerances, probe seeds, recomputation frequency, and solver cross-checks.
Group definitions can be circular or off-manifold. Fix them before branches, bound transformations to valid input ranges, include natural strata, and blind the semantic audit.
Output-outlier progress can mean memorizing wrong labels. Keep corrupted-label fit separate from clean, balanced, tail, and robustness endpoints.
Full-batch results may disappear under stochastic or optimizer-state dynamics. Treat each operator as a separate estimand, not an ablation that can be pooled after failure.
Many checkpoint-by-group contrasts create multiplicity and dependence. Freeze the primary vector, use hierarchical paired analysis, and publish the full contrast family.
A stable one-mode mechanism at small width may become multi-mode at scale. Require rank-r and held-out projector gates before architecture or scale language.
first_week: Implement full-Hessian and Lanczos eigenspaces, projector overlap, localization, grad S, exact Q_k, C_k, and finite-difference checks on one smooth full-batch model.
Reproduce one same-checkpoint eta versus eta/2 allocation result and verify that effective-time normalization does not remove ordinary branch differences.
Implement rank-one and rank-r sharp clamps, random- and stable-subspace clamps, removed-energy replay, and constrained norm-plus-linear-progress compensation with logged residuals.
Freeze mechanically defined inlier, boundary, randomized-label, valid coherent-shift, random-shift, rare, and natural margin-decile groups before running intervention branches.
Branch at least 12 seed-checkpoint blocks to estimate paired variance, projector stability, matching feasibility, third-derivative cost, and a minimum meaningful effect for preregistration.

Preregister the primary allocation vector, abstention rules, solver tolerances, rank choice, matching hierarchy, future-data schedule, held-out width and architecture, multiplicity correction, and all decisive falsifiers.

competitive_landscape.title: Edge of Stability Selectively Shapes Learning Across the Data Distribution
competitive_landscape.difference: It branches from one checkpoint by halving eta and measures top-mode alignment; this proposal holds nominal eta fixed, intervenes only on the unstable subspace, matches ordinary update effects, and tests exact Q_k against C_k.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: It establishes global loss and sharpness behavior near 2/eta; the proposal asks a narrower post-entry causal question about heterogeneous group progress.

competitive_landscape.title: Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: It derives cubic feedback and implicit bias near EoS; this proposal tests whether the resulting sharpness term has a causal, group-specific allocation effect under a mode clamp.

competitive_landscape.title: Edge of Stochastic Stability: Revisiting the Edge of Stability for SGD
competitive_landscape.difference: It replaces full-Hessian sharpness with a batch-distribution-aware SGD quantity; the proposal therefore blocks SGD transfer until its clamp uses that stochastic operator.

competitive_landscape.title: Momentum Further Constrains Sharpness at the Edge of Stochastic Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: It predicts momentum- and batch-dependent plateaus; this proposal treats momentum as a separate state-space or stochastic intervention rather than reusing 2/eta and Euclidean v_1.

competitive_landscape.title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Operates at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: It generalizes EoS to non-Euclidean and preconditioned updates; the proposal uses that distinction as a gate against transferring a Euclidean clamp to Adam.

competitive_landscape.title: Characterizing Optimizer-Dependent Training Dynamics Through Hessian Eigenvector Displacement and Localization
competitive_landscape.difference: It reports increasingly stable leading directions under SGD but stronger reorganization and localization under Adam; this proposal makes projector stability and localization explicit validity gates rather than assuming a persistent v_1.

competitive_landscape.title: Zeroth-Order Optimization at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.relationship: full-spectrum ZO counterexample to lambda-max transfer
competitive_landscape.difference: It shows mean-square ZO stability depends on the entire Hessian spectrum and tractable bounds use lambda_max plus trace; the proposal explicitly forbids claiming ZO transfer from a first-order top-mode clamp.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Preconditioners Trigger Loss Spikes in Adam
competitive_landscape.difference: It attributes spikes to lagging second moments and the preconditioned Hessian; the proposal requires an Adam-specific metric and does not interpret raw-Hessian damping as optimizer-generic.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Gradient Descent on Edge of Stability in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: It studies convergence under structural assumptions; the proposal tests a randomized finite-horizon subgroup estimand and publishes matching and Taylor residuals rather than inferring from a local threshold alone.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Edge-of-Stability Training Dynamics with a Minimalist Example
competitive_landscape.difference: It proves global EoS behavior in a low-dimensional model; the proposal uses smooth minimalist models only to validate the intervention before testing data-distribution heterogeneity.

competitive_landscape.title: Outliers with Opposing Signals Have an Outsized Effect on Neural Network Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: It shows opposing-signal outliers can disproportionately shape optimization; the proposal includes group-gradient, label-noise, and difficulty baselines so an outlier effect is not mislabeled as EoS-specific allocation.

competitive_landscape.title: The Origin of Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: It derives segment-Hessian and step-energy identities but no subgroup intervention; the proposal uses finite-step residual accounting while refusing to treat a conditional weighted asymptote as causal allocation.

competitive_landscape.title: Weight-norm Criticality: A Mechanism for Loss Spikes Induced by the Normalization and Weight Decay
competitive_landscape.difference: It links normalized-block contraction to curvature and disables module weight decay; the proposal holds regularization fixed, treats norm boundaries as gauge-sensitive, and directly intervenes on post-entry curvature.

competitive_landscape.title: Conservation Law Breaking at the Edge of Stability: A Spectral Theory of Non-Convex Neural Network Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: It studies aggregate layer-balance drift with a fixed-mode spectral closure; the proposal does not infer subgroup allocation from conservation drift and instead uses randomized same-checkpoint causal branches.

brief.novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after four hash-pinned, page-anchored readings and direct inspection of 20 unique primary competitors: global and stochastic EoS, cubic self-stabilization, minimalist bifurcations, outlier-driven optimization, non-Euclidean and momentum boundaries, Adam preconditioned spikes, optimizer-dependent eigenspace displacement and localization, ZO full-spectrum stability, norm criticality, exact finite-step balances, and conservation-law breaking are established. The defensible contribution is not another transition forecast, critical norm, subgroup score, learning-rate controller, or generic optimizer certificate. It is a narrow post-entry causal test: hold eta and data fixed, selectively remove unstable-subspace dynamics, match ordinary update effects, and ask whether the signed distribution of group progress changes as exact Q predicts. If that boundary cannot be maintained, the proposal duplicates the prospective criticality tournament and should be rejected.
brief.evidence_note: Supported by four current full-text readings totaling 83 pages, with 49 page-anchored findings, 115 anchors, and 40 checked competitor entries spanning 18 unique primary papers, plus direct current-arXiv inspection of optimizer-dependent eigenspace dynamics (arxiv:2606.30226) and full-spectrum ZO stability (arxiv:2604.14669). The scope is deliberately post-entry subgroup allocation: no transition forecasting, trigger discovery, learning-rate-controller ranking, or generic update certificate is included.

factors.rationale: Requires a fresh experimental scaffold derived from public paper specifications.
Frozen feature extraction and analytic heads are economical, but paired domain orders, DINOv2 transfer, trigger calibration, and full replay-state rebuilding require a moderate replicated sweep.
Fixed bytes, equal swap counts, frozen triggers, paired task orders, calibrated event prediction, and joint oracle gaps give unusually crisp comparisons.

Dynamic adapters, analytic projections, random-feature compression, replay, and eviction are established; the narrow novelty is activation-aware fixed-budget basis replacement with state-correct replay.
ImageNet-R can reject the trigger and replacement logic quickly, while robust conclusions require held-out domain orders and a second backbone.

assumptions: A small latent coreset may be stored, but every persistent byte in the projection, inverse Gram matrix, classifier, adapters, and coreset counts against one fixed budget.
A replaced basis block invalidates accumulated sufficient statistics, so the analytic state must be rebuilt from state-correct latent replay rather than algebraically patched without evidence.
The trigger is calibrated only on a development stream and frozen before held-out domain orders and backbone changes.
Spectral contraction is useful only together with top-mode activation and loss scale; spectral radius alone is not treated as a forgetting predictor.

brief.title: Activation-aware basis garbage collection for fixed-budget continual representations
brief.thesis: Keep a random-feature representation at fixed width and replace equal-size basis blocks only when a frozen score combining estimated contraction, top-mode activation, loss scale, and representation drift predicts that later domains need missing directions. Rebuild the analytic head from a byte-matched latent coreset after every swap, and require the learned trigger to beat equal-count periodic replacement.
brief.motivation: Initial-task-guided random projections can be compact but freeze the representation before later classes arrive, while expandable adapters and continually updated analytic projections spend growing or differently structured state. The spectral forgetting theory shows why contraction alone is insufficient, C-Flat Turbo shows that cached update directions can be refreshed, and Neural Garbage Collection shows how task reward can govern eviction. The open question is whether basis capacity itself can be garbage-collected under an exact memory budget without turning replay or refresh frequency into the hidden advantage.
brief.research_question: Can an activation-aware, prospectively calibrated trigger decide when and which random-feature blocks to replace so that a fixed-byte continual learner improves worst-domain retention and forward transfer beyond periodic replacement, replay alone, and existing fixed or growing analytic representations?
non_claims: The project does not claim random projections, analytic recursive classifiers, low-rank compression, adapter growth, coreset replay, or learned eviction as new.
The shared-solution linear spectral law is a source of candidate features, not a theorem for nonlinear domain-incremental learning.
Exemplar-free does not mean memory-free: dense inverse-Gram state, projection weights, adapters, and latent replay all count.
Beating a joint linear probe is not beating joint full fine-tuning or a general continual-learning upper bound.
subquestions: Does contraction plus top-mode activation and loss scale predict harmful representation mismatch better than loss, covariance drift, principal angle, or spectral radius alone?
Does learned timing matter after periodic replacement is matched on the exact number and size of swaps?
Are gains caused by new basis directions, the latent coreset needed to rebuild state, or both?
Does the trigger transfer without recalibration across task order, DomainNet domains, and a DINOv2 backbone?
What fixed-byte allocation among projection width, quadratic sufficient statistics, adapters, and replay gives the best retention-forward-transfer frontier?
method: Start from first-session adaptation plus a compact guided random projection and recursive ridge head. Partition the projection into equal-size replaceable blocks and expose exact persistent-byte accounting.

Estimate a low-rank task-projection operator from streamed latent features; combine its contraction estimate with target activation coefficients, empirical loss scale, covariance drift, and principal-angle change in a prespecified sparse trigger.
When triggered, score candidate random blocks on current residual improvement plus held-out coreset preservation, evict the least jointly useful block, and keep width and persistent bytes fixed.

Store a byte-matched latent coreset with labels and provenance. After each basis swap, recompute all retained latent features and rebuild the inverse Gram matrix and analytic classifier from scratch so state corresponds to the current basis.
Calibrate feature definitions and thresholds on ImageNet-R only, freeze them, and evaluate paired unseen DomainNet domain orders and DINOv2 without recalibration.
Separate trigger value from replacement value with equal-count periodic and random schedules, and separate basis value from replay value with no-replay, replay-only, and swap-only arms.

scaling_claim_protocol.answer: ImageNet-R is a development environment, not evidence of general continual adaptation. Freeze the complete trigger, byte allocation, and replacement policy before DomainNet orders and the DINOv2 backbone are opened.
supporting_evidence: The frozen score improves Brier error by at least 10% and its AUROC lower confidence bound exceeds every scalar trigger
Worst-domain final accuracy improves by at least 1.0 point with a paired 95% confidence interval above zero
Periodic equal-count replacement trails by more than 0.3 accuracy points under identical bytes and compute exposure
Gains persist after coreset bytes are equalized and on DINOv2 without trigger recalibration
Forgetting does not worsen by more than 0.5 points and wall-clock stays within 1.25 times periodic replacement
claim_blockers: The multivariate score does not improve Brier error by 10% or cannot beat the best scalar trigger
Periodic equal-count swaps match within 0.3 accuracy points
The worst-domain confidence interval includes zero or the gain is below 1.0 point
Any arm exceeds the persistent-byte budget by more than 2%
Benefits disappear after latent-coreset allocation is equalized or reverse on DINOv2
Analytic-state rebuild cost exceeds the registered wall-clock ceiling
prospective_design: Tune projection width, coreset allocation, trigger sparsity, and thresholds on ImageNet-R only
Freeze five task-order seeds, byte accounting, refresh budget, and all event labels before held-out evaluation
Open DomainNet orders first and DINOv2 as a second untouched transfer gate
Publish every trigger, rejected swap, rebuild cost, and byte ledger
why_small_models_fail: Quadratic inverse-Gram state changes the optimal width-memory tradeoff as feature dimension grows
A privileged initial task can cover later ImageNet-R classes but fail under true domain shift
Spectral modes and their activated coefficients change with backbone representation geometry
A coreset that is adequate for one swap frequency can become stale under frequent basis replacement
scaling_claim_protocol.claim_language: If only ImageNet-R passes, claim a development-set replacement result. Claim transferable fixed-budget basis adaptation only if the frozen DomainNet and DINOv2 gates pass.

experiment.primary_hypothesis: Under equal persistent bytes and equal swap counts, the frozen activation-aware trigger will improve worst-domain final accuracy by at least 1.0 point over periodic replacement while keeping average forgetting within 0.5 points.
experiment.secondary_hypothesis: The trigger will reduce calibrated harmful-mismatch prediction error by at least 10% relative to spectral radius, loss, covariance drift, and principal angle alone, and this calibration will transfer to DINOv2 without refitting.
experiment.primary_outcome: The paired worst-domain final-accuracy difference between frozen activation-aware and equal-count periodic replacement under the fixed persistent-byte budget, with average forgetting, trigger calibration, and DINOv2 transfer as hard gates.
domains: ImageNet-R class-incremental streams for development and trigger calibration
Held-out DomainNet domain-incremental orders with five paired seeds
ViT-B/16 and an untouched DINOv2 backbone
Synthetic shared-solution and target-shift linear streams as positive and negative controls for the spectral features
baselines: Frozen compact guided projection, RanPAC, LoRanPAC, AnaCP, EASE, G-ACIL, ACIL, and first-session adaptation
Periodic equal-count replacement, random replacement, no replacement, and replacement with a random trigger
Spectral-radius-only, loss-only, covariance-drift, principal-angle, and sparse multivariate triggers
No replay, latent replay without basis swaps, swaps without replay, and byte-matched replay plus swaps
Joint linear probe and joint full-fine-tuning references reported separately
ablations: Remove contraction, activation coefficient, loss-scale, covariance, and principal-angle features one at a time
Hold swap count fixed while changing only timing
Hold the trigger fixed while comparing residual, preservation, and random block eviction
Vary byte allocation among projection width, inverse-Gram state, adapters, and coreset
Patch analytic state approximately versus rebuild it exactly from replay
Calibrate per-domain versus use the prospectively frozen trigger
experiment.decision_rule: Pass only if the frozen trigger clears both its calibration gate and the paired worst-domain accuracy gate, periodic equal-count replacement falls outside the 0.3-point equivalence margin, all methods stay within 2% of the byte budget, and the result survives DINOv2. Otherwise attribute any gain to replay, refresh count, or development-set tuning rather than adaptive basis garbage collection.

evaluation: Final and stage-average accuracy, worst-domain accuracy, average forgetting, backward transfer, and forward transfer
Gap to matched joint linear and joint full-fine-tuning references
Trigger AUROC, AUPRC, Brier score, calibration error, lead time, and false-refresh rate
Persistent bytes by projection, inverse Gram matrix, classifier, adapters, and coreset, plus peak workspace
Wall-clock, feature-extraction FLOPs, analytic rebuild FLOPs, refresh count, and rejected candidate count
Condition number, numerical failures, active-rank coverage, and later-domain residual reduction
Paired task-order confidence intervals and sensitivity to initial-domain privilege
risks: The linear spectral features may not transfer to nonlinear frozen representations. Include synthetic positive controls and require incremental calibration value before interpreting them.
Rebuilding the inverse Gram state can dominate runtime. Measure it separately and cap total wall-clock relative to periodic refresh.
A latent coreset may carry most of the gain. Equalize its bytes and include replay-only and swap-only factorial arms.
Block replacement may make old sufficient statistics invalid even with replay. Recompute features and analytic state from the current basis after every accepted swap.
Exact byte matching can disadvantage methods with different state structures. Report a budget frontier in addition to one registered operating point.
Task-boundary access can overstate applicability. Describe the result as boundary-aware and leave streaming change-point detection outside the claim.
first_week: Implement byte-exact accounting for a frozen random projection, dense inverse Gram matrix, classifier, and latent coreset.
Add block replacement followed by a from-scratch state rebuild and verify equivalence to batch ridge on retained latent examples.
Create periodic, random, no-swap, replay-only, and swap-only arms with identical exposure and persistent bytes.
Estimate contraction, activation, loss-scale, covariance, and principal-angle features on one ImageNet-R stream and measure their event-label stability.
Preregister the event definition, sparse trigger, swap budget, five paired orders, byte tolerance, equivalence margin, and DINOv2 transfer gate.

competitive_landscape.title: RanPAC: Random Projections and Pre-trained Models for Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: RanPAC freezes a large unguided random lift. The proposal keeps width fixed but changes which blocks occupy that capacity under a prospectively frozen trigger.

competitive_landscape.title: LoRanPAC: Low-Rank Random Features and Pre-Trained Models for Bridging Theory and Practice in Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: LoRanPAC controls a very wide random lift through continual low-rank factorization. The proposal tests active basis turnover under the same total-byte constraint.

competitive_landscape.title: AnaCP: Toward Upper-Bound Continual Learning via Analytic Contrastive Projection
competitive_landscape.difference: AnaCP updates a contrastive analytic projection toward joint-training geometry. The proposed method uses discrete fixed-width block replacement and explicit replay-correct state rebuilding.

competitive_landscape.title: Expandable Subspace Ensemble for Pre-Trained Model-Based Class-Incremental Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: EASE adds task-specific adapter subspaces as stages arrive. The proposal forbids growth and asks which existing basis capacity should be evicted.

competitive_landscape.title: GACL: Exemplar-Free Generalized Analytic Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: G-ACIL provides recursive equivalence in generalized class-incremental learning but does not adapt its feature basis through fixed-budget replacement.

competitive_landscape.title: ACIL: Analytic Class-Incremental Learning with Absolute Memorization and Privacy Protection
competitive_landscape.difference: ACIL establishes recursive ridge updates with a random buffer layer. The proposal makes representation state replaceable and therefore must rebuild those statistics correctly.

competitive_landscape.title: First Session Adaptation: A Strong Replay-Free Baseline for Class-Incremental Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: First Session Adaptation exposes how much a privileged initial task already provides. Held-out domain orders test whether basis replacement adds value beyond that privilege.

brief.novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after four hash-pinned, page-anchored readings and the brief- plus reading-level competitor panels: initial-session adaptation, frozen and low-rank random features, continually updated analytic projections, growing adapter subspaces, recursive analytic classifiers, latent replay, cached optimizer directions, and learned cache eviction are established. Spectral forgetting and guided random projection directly motivate the representation and state questions; cached optimizer directions and learned KV-cache eviction are adjacent trigger or resource-allocation analogies, not direct evidence for basis replacement. The defensible contribution is a fixed-byte representation in which a prospectively calibrated activation-aware trigger replaces equal-size basis blocks and reconstructs mathematically valid analytic state from byte-matched replay.
brief.evidence_note: The four full-text readings total 88 pages, 49 page-anchored findings, and 33 checked primary-source competitor records, but their support is tiered. arxiv:2604.13460 and arxiv:2603.19145 directly support spectral forgetting and guided random-feature allocation. arxiv:2604.11064 contributes only an adjacent state-trigger and cached-direction analogy, while arxiv:2604.18002 contributes only an adjacent fixed-budget eviction analogy; neither directly demonstrates replaceable analytic bases.

factors.rationale: Requires a fresh experimental scaffold derived from public paper specifications.
Symbolic object-state trajectories are cheap to generate, and a useful pilot fits small transformers; long rollout grids and perception-noise replication add moderate cost.
Known symmetry transforms, exogenous breaker masks, controlled interventions, and held-out breaker compositions give direct pass/fail tests instead of relying on average rollout error.
Exact, approximate, residual, and regularized equivariance are established; the narrower delta is a causal certificate that localizes and calibrates broken symmetry against the true exogenous cause.
A wall-plus-gravity pilot can falsify the localization claim quickly, while unseen compositions, long-horizon control, and noisy-slot replication take longer.

assumptions: The simulator exposes exact symmetry-preserving events and the walls, fields, contacts, or material anisotropies that break each candidate symmetry.
Hard-equivariant models can receive the same exogenous context as soft models, preventing hidden context from becoming an unfair architectural advantage.
Model and augmentation comparisons can be matched on data, parameters, optimizer search, training FLOPs, and rollout budget.
A soft-equivariance claim requires calibrated event-level residuals and intervention behavior, not only lower aggregate prediction error.

brief.title: Where symmetry breaks: causal localization certificates for soft geometric world models
brief.thesis: A soft geometric world model should remain equivariant on symmetry-preserving transitions and spend its non-equivariant capacity only where an exogenous wall, field, contact, or anisotropic material actually breaks the symmetry. Test that claim with transformed orbit pairs and selective counterfactuals: residual magnitude and location must track the true breaker, change correctly when the breaker is intervened on, transfer to unseen breaker compositions, and improve long-horizon prediction or control beyond a correctly contextualized exact model.
brief.motivation: Recent Clifford world models improve long autoregressive rollouts when boundaries and gravity make exact global equivariance wrong, but their non-equivariant projections do not reveal whether the model learned the broken symmetry or merely gained useful capacity. Existing residual, regularized, and approximately equivariant networks likewise establish that softness can help without certifying where or why it helps. A causal localization benchmark would turn soft equivariance from an architectural label into a falsifiable representation claim.
brief.research_question: Can a soft geometric dynamics model identify, localize, and causally respond to the actual exogenous sources of symmetry breaking while preserving equivariance everywhere else?
non_claims: Soft, residual, regularized, mixed, and approximate equivariance are established ideas; proposing another relaxed layer is not the contribution.
Lower in-distribution rollout error does not show that a model localized a broken symmetry.
An exact-equivariant baseline deprived of wall or field context is not a fair test of whether softness is necessary.
Oracle object-state success does not establish object discovery or tracking from pixels.
subquestions: Does the learned equivariance residual vanish on symmetry-preserving events and increase monotonically with known breaker strength?
Can residual attribution identify the correct object, interaction, time, and exogenous context rather than correlating with generic prediction difficulty?
Do wall, gravity, and friction interventions change residuals and predictions in the simulator-correct direction without retraining?
Does calibrated localization survive unseen breaker combinations, object counts, materials, and a noisy discovered-slot input?
method: Build factorial JAX2D or Kinetix worlds with independently controlled walls, uniform and spatially varying fields, anisotropic friction, contacts, object counts, and materials. Record exact event masks and breaker strength for every transition.

Generate E(2) orbit pairs for symmetry-preserving transitions and selective counterfactuals that transform object state while either holding breaker context fixed or transforming it consistently. This separates genuine equivariance, conditional equivariance, and correctly broken symmetry.

Compare an exact equivariant model without context, an exact or conditional equivariant model with wall and field tokens, residual-path and regularized soft models, S and S-Ad Clifford transformers, and ordinary augmented transformers under matched parameters, data, optimizer search, and training FLOPs.

Expose or estimate a per-object, per-edge, per-time equivariance residual. Calibrate it against the simulator's breaker mask and magnitude, then intervene on wall position, field direction, or material anisotropy while holding the observed state fixed.
Repeat the registered tests first with oracle objects and then with noisy tracked or discovered slots so failures in dynamics are not confused with failures in perception.

validation_funnel.gate: Every candidate soft model must match the exact model's orbit consistency and rollout quality when no breaker is present; extra capacity cannot silently degrade the symmetric regime.
Event-level residuals must identify the correct object, interaction, and time and remain calibrated across registered breaker-strength sweeps beyond prediction-error and contact-frequency baselines.
Holding object state fixed while changing wall, field, or material context must move both the residual and next-state prediction in the simulator-correct direction.
Localization must transfer to untouched breaker combinations and yield better 50-to-200-step rollouts or closed-loop planning than the best correctly contextualized exact model at matched resources.

experiment.primary_hypothesis: A residual or regularized soft geometric model will preserve near-exact equivariance away from exogenous breakers while its localized residual tracks breaker identity and strength and causally improves predictions on broken-symmetry events.
experiment.secondary_hypothesis: A correctly contextualized exact-equivariant model will close part of the apparent soft-model advantage, but calibrated residual models will retain an advantage on unseen combinations of multiple local breakers.
experiment.primary_outcome: Event-level breaker localization and strength calibration under untouched context interventions, followed by long-horizon rollout or control improvement over the best resource-matched contextual exact model while preserving the registered symmetric-regime equivariance tolerance.
domains: Rigid-body collisions with and without local walls
Projectile and support dynamics under controllable gravity fields
Sliding and contact under isotropic versus anisotropic friction
Mixed wall, field, and material worlds with held-out compositions
baselines: Exact EGNN or Clifford-equivariant dynamics without breaker context
Exact conditional-equivariant dynamics with wall, field, and material tokens
Residual Pathway Prior and regularized approximate-equivariance models
S and S-Ad soft Clifford transformers
Ordinary graph or object transformer with registered geometric augmentation
Prediction-error, contact-frequency, and oracle breaker-mask attribution baselines
ablations: Hide versus expose breaker context to every architecture
Hold versus consistently transform exogenous context in orbit pairs
Remove residual sparsity, locality, or calibration losses one at a time
Match epochs only versus match examples, training FLOPs, and search budget
Train on isolated breakers versus registered combinations
Replace oracle objects with tracked and discovered noisy slots
experiment.decision_rule: Pass only if the soft model preserves the registered symmetric-regime tolerance, localizes breaker identity, object, interaction, and time above all error-based controls, changes correctly under untouched context interventions, transfers to unseen breaker compositions, and improves long-horizon rollout or control over the best resource-matched contextual exact model. Otherwise report a capacity or interpolation gain, not learned soft geometry.

evaluation: Orbit-consistency error on strictly symmetry-preserving transitions
Breaker-mask precision-recall and object, edge, and time localization error
Residual calibration and monotonicity over wall, field, and anisotropy strength
Counterfactual next-state accuracy after wall, gravity, and material interventions
Held-out breaker-composition, object-count, material, and spatial-layout generalization
One-step error plus 50-, 100-, and 200-step stability, conservation, contact timing, and planning return
Parameters, examples, optimizer trials, training FLOPs, inference latency, and seed uncertainty
risks: Residual magnitude may simply track hard examples. Compare against calibrated prediction-error, uncertainty, contact-density, and unrestricted-capacity controls and require context interventions.

Global transforms can move walls out of frame or alter boundary conditions. Generate paired worlds from an explicit group action over both state and context and separately register the held-context counterfactual.
A contextual exact model may be expressive enough to remove the soft-model advantage. That is a useful negative result: it identifies missing context rather than a need for relaxed symmetry.
Long rollouts can amplify tiny local errors unrelated to geometry. Report event-conditioned one-step calibration alongside horizon curves and conservation diagnostics.
Oracle entity inputs make the task unrealistically clean. Treat them as the dynamics isolation stage and require a noisy-slot replication before making perception-level claims.
Sparse residual penalties may manufacture visually appealing localization. Predeclare calibration and intervention gates that a sparse but incorrect explanation cannot pass.
first_week: Implement two-body collisions with optional wall and gravity context and emit exact event and breaker annotations.
Generate symmetry-preserving orbit pairs plus held-context and transformed-context counterfactual pairs.
Train one exact contextual model, one residual soft model, and one ordinary augmented transformer at matched parameters and examples.
Measure orbit error, breaker localization, strength calibration, and wall or field swap intervention accuracy before any long rollout claim.
Preregister the unseen wall-plus-gravity composition, compute budget, symmetric-regime tolerance, and causal pass rule.

competitive_landscape.title: Residual Pathway Priors for Soft Equivariance Constraints
competitive_landscape.difference: Residual paths already turn hard equivariance into a tunable prior. The proposed certificate tests whether residual use is localized, calibrated, and causally tied to the true exogenous breaker.

competitive_landscape.title: Regularizing Towards Soft Equivariance Under Mixed Symmetries
competitive_landscape.difference: This work regularizes toward candidate symmetries under mixed regimes. The proposal adds exact event labels, context interventions, unseen breaker compositions, and long-horizon utility gates.

competitive_landscape.title: Approximately Equivariant Networks for Imperfectly Symmetric Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Approximately equivariant networks establish benefits when symmetry is imperfect. They do not by themselves certify where the symmetry fails or whether the model responds to the causal breaker.

competitive_landscape.title: Geometric Algebra Transformer
competitive_landscape.difference: GATr supplies exact geometric-algebra attention. It is a hard-equivariant baseline and implementation substrate, not an event-level broken-symmetry certificate.

competitive_landscape.title: Clifford Group Equivariant Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: CGENNs derive exact group-equivariant Clifford operations. The proposal tests when relaxing those operations is necessary after the same breaker context is supplied.

competitive_landscape.title: E(n) Equivariant Graph Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: EGNN demonstrates exact E(n)-equivariant particle dynamics. A context-conditioned EGNN is the critical baseline for separating missing context from a true need for soft symmetry.

competitive_landscape.title: Does equivariance matter at scale?
competitive_landscape.difference: This study shows augmentation and scale can close equivariance gains. The proposed benchmark therefore matches FLOPs and search and requires transfer and intervention evidence beyond epoch efficiency.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to Simulate Complex Physics with Graph Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Graph Network-based Simulators provide a strong long-rollout physics baseline without Clifford structure. They test whether the certificate buys utility rather than only interpretability.

competitive_landscape.title: SlotFormer: Unsupervised Visual Dynamics Simulation with Object-Centric Models
competitive_landscape.difference: SlotFormer learns dynamics over discovered visual slots. It motivates the required noisy-slot replication after oracle-state dynamics have been isolated.

competitive_landscape.title: Contrastive Learning of Structured World Models
competitive_landscape.difference: C-SWM tests learned object-factorized transitions and composition from pixels. The proposal instead audits conditional group structure and causal localization of known symmetry breakers.

competitive_landscape.title: When Do Neural Networks Learn World Models?
competitive_landscape.difference: This work formalizes when structured world-model solutions beat memorization. The proposed study adds an empirical causal test of which parts of the learned dynamics obey or violate a registered symmetry.

brief.novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after four hash-pinned, page-anchored readings and a 41-entry primary-source audit spanning 35 unique papers: exact geometric attention, Clifford equivariance, residual and regularized soft equivariance, approximately equivariant dynamics, object-centric simulation, and data-compute comparisons are established. The defensible contribution is a prospective causal certificate that requires the non-equivariant residual to localize the true breaker, calibrate to its strength, respond correctly to interventions, transfer compositionally, and outperform a correctly contextualized exact model. Another soft layer or in-distribution rollout leaderboard would not be novel.
brief.evidence_note: Supported by four current full-text readings totaling 72 pages, with 60 page-anchored findings, 21 evaluation audits, 45 limitations, 40 failure modes, and 41 directly inspected competitor entries spanning 35 unique primary IDs.

factors.rationale: Requires a fresh experimental scaffold derived from public paper specifications.

The primary factorial can use fully generated corpora and 20M-50M parameter decoders, but credible seed intervals, mid-run switches, tied and untied embeddings, and one frozen larger confirmation create a meaningful compute bill.

Corpus statistics are exactly auditable, signature predictions are frozen before training, and parameter, regional, local-dimension, and native-behavior outcomes have explicit sham, clamp, rescue, and shuffled-prediction controls.

Co-occurrence geometry, anisotropy, intrinsic dimension, local manifolds, and representation decomposition are crowded. The defensible novelty is the preregistered corpus-transition intervention and causal transport chain, not any individual geometry statistic.
A two-matrix synthetic pilot can reject the signature-to-geometry link in days, while behavior mediation, estimator robustness, and the held-out scale gate require longer multi-seed runs.

assumptions: Paired corpus generators can change selected conditional transitions while exactly matching vocabulary, stationary unigram mass, sequence length, position counts, entropy strata, and the latent propositions tested by the common evaluator.
Repeated small-decoder runs can be matched closely enough in tokens, FLOPs, optimizer state, initialization distribution, and achieved pre-switch loss to identify the randomized corpus treatment.
Region and intrinsic-dimension estimates can be cross-fitted on held-out activations and reported as estimator-indexed measurements rather than treated as absolute properties of text.
A frozen larger-model confirmation is affordable only after the small factorial and causal clamp/rescue gates pass.

brief.title: Same tokens, different transitions: causal transport of representation geometry
brief.thesis: Randomize conditional transition structure while holding token marginals, length, position, entropy strata, latent propositions, architecture, and training budget fixed. Before training, use the induced conditional-distribution change to predict which embedding relations should move; then require that movement to propagate prospectively into held-out contextual regions, estimator-robust local dimension, and native behavior. Mid-run switches, sham switches, geometry clamps, and geometry rescues distinguish a causal transport chain from a post hoc geometric description.
brief.motivation: Probability Signature derives conditional-distribution terms in embedding and unembedding gradients and observes them in small decoders, but its natural-language evidence is correlational and leaves attention and higher-order terms unresolved. Isotropy in Contextual Embedding Space shows that global anisotropy can hide separated regions and local manifolds, yet centered mean cosine is weaker than true covariance isotropy and no behavior is tested. Directions to Regions finds useful local low-rank activation regions, but its regions are distribution-bound and its strongest causal tasks use supervised selection. Intrinsic Dimension of Texts separates local dimension from entropy, compression, linear dimension, and isotropy, while leaving genre and feature interventions causally underidentified. Together they motivate a controlled transition intervention that predicts geometry before training and blocks the claim unless geometry matters for behavior.
brief.research_question: When vocabulary, marginals, entropy, position, latent task semantics, compute, and initialization are matched, do controlled changes in corpus conditionals cause prospectively predictable transport from embedding geometry to contextual regions and local intrinsic dimension, and does that transport mediate held-out native behavior?
non_claims: Conditional distributions, co-occurrence matrices, embedding anisotropy, local manifolds, intrinsic-dimension estimators, mixture models, and causal mediation are not new individually.
Near-zero centered cosine is not called isotropy unless held-out covariance-spectrum and uniformity tests also pass.
A local intrinsic-dimension estimate is an estimator-, layer-, tokenizer-, corpus-, and model-indexed measurement, not an intrinsic scalar property of raw text.
Predicting a rotation or cluster movement without a native-behavior consequence does not establish a functional representation mechanism.
A successful small synthetic model does not establish natural-language or large-scale transfer without the frozen confirmation gate.
subquestions: Which adjacent-token, reverse-token, position-conditioned, and longer-context signatures prospectively predict embedding and unembedding movement after matched corpus rewiring?
Do parameter-level movements precede and predict held-out changes in contextual centroids, tangent subspaces, neighborhood topology, and multiple local-dimension estimators?
Does clamping the predicted geometry attenuate a behavioral treatment effect, and can imposing the predicted geometry without the corpus switch partially rescue it?
Are apparent region or dimension changes explained instead by token frequency, absolute position, likelihood, norm, rogue coordinates, tokenizer fragmentation, or achieved training loss?
Do the direction, rank order, and calibration of frozen predictions survive an untouched corpus family, larger width, tied-versus-untied embeddings, and a later training regime?
method: Construct two independently generated corpus families. The first uses degree-preserving rewires of stationary Markov chains with identical token marginals and matched row-entropy spectra. The second expresses the same latent propositions through counterbalanced templates and token codebooks, matching vocabulary, length, position, punctuation, and tokenizer counts while changing selected transition conditionals.

Hash every corpus and publish an exact balance audit. Before any model is trained, compute adjacent, reverse, position-conditioned, and longer-context probability-signature deltas and freeze predicted pairwise embedding/unembedding movements plus explicit abstention rules for poorly estimated pairs.

Train tied- and untied-embedding 20M-50M parameter decoders across at least eight seeds per primary cell with matched initialization distributions, examples, tokens, optimizer, schedule, FLOPs, and evaluation cadence. Register equal-compute and equal-achieved-loss estimands separately.

At prespecified checkpoints, randomize replicas to the true conditional switch, a no-op continuation, a byte-identical loader restart, a marginal-only perturbation, a position-only perturbation, or a signature-shuffled switch. Use pre-switch checkpoints as paired blocks.

Track embedding and unembedding Gram movement, centered within-region covariance spectra, held-out cluster assignments, MFA centroids and subspace spans, neighborhood overlap, rogue-coordinate sensitivity, PCA dimension, and PHD, MLE, TLE, and TwoNN local dimension. Cross-fit every learned partition and report estimator disagreement.

Measure native behavior with a shared sealed evaluator over held-out continuation, paraphrase-invariant proposition recovery, compositional path completion, and multi-hop queries whose latent answers are identical across corpus arms. Geometry-only probes are secondary outcomes.

Run a causal mediation gate: penalize predicted Gram movement after the true switch, impose the predicted target geometry without switching data, and use norm-, rank-, and loss-matched random transports. Claim transport only if the randomized treatment moves geometry first, clamp attenuates behavior, rescue improves it, and random transports do not.

scaling_claim_protocol.answer: The small factorial can identify a mechanism in a controlled generator, not scaling. Freeze corpus construction, signature estimator, geometry endpoints, abstention rules, intervention coefficients, and decision thresholds before opening an untouched corpus family and a larger decoder.
supporting_evidence: Frozen signature deltas predict held-out parameter movement beyond marginals, position, loss, norm, and shuffled-signature baselines across seeds and both corpus families.
Parameter movement temporally precedes and predicts regional and local-dimension movement under cross-fitted diagnostics.
The true switch changes sealed native behavior; a geometry clamp attenuates that effect and a geometry rescue recovers part of it without a comparable loss or norm change.
Prediction direction, calibration, and behavioral mediation survive tied and untied embeddings, later checkpoints, an untouched generator, and a preregistered larger width.
The result remains after rogue-coordinate removal, alternative clustering, multiple intrinsic-dimension estimators, and likelihood-based abstention.
claim_blockers: Marginal-only, position-only, achieved-loss, or shuffled-signature baselines predict movement equally well.
The effect exists only for in-sample clusters, one intrinsic-dimension estimator, one seed, or one convenient layer.
Geometry changes after behavior, or changes without any sealed native-behavior consequence.
The clamp leaves behavior unchanged, the rescue fails, or random norm-matched transports perform equally well.
Prediction rank order reverses at later training, in the untouched generator, or at the frozen larger scale.
Corpus balance audits reveal unmatched propositions, tokenizer counts, entropy, position, contamination, or training compute.
prospective_design: Develop the generator and balance tests on one Markov family and reserve a second transition family unopened.
Freeze signature definitions, pair-selection rules, geometry metrics, layers, seeds, behavioral tasks, and all exclusion rules before training the held-out family.
Run the complete small factorial and causal clamp/rescue analysis before selecting one fixed intervention for the larger model.
Publish null pairs, abstentions, estimator disagreements, all seed trajectories, corpus hashes, and the untouched larger result.
why_small_models_fail: Small-initialization expansions can be overwhelmed later by attention, normalization, optimizer history, and higher-order residual-network terms.
Synthetic stationary chains provide exact balance and known semantics that natural corpora cannot match.
Local regions, neighborhood density, and intrinsic dimension can change with width, tokenizer, layer, or corpus even when behavior is stable.
A larger pretrained model may already encode the sealed propositions, turning the intervention into retrieval or fine-tuning rather than representation formation.
scaling_claim_protocol.claim_language: If only the controlled factorial passes, claim causal representation transport in those generated corpora. Claim scale robustness only if the frozen larger run preserves prediction calibration and the clamp/rescue behavior gate; never infer web-scale natural-language universality from geometry alone.
